    Neurons transport their messages when they are stimulated by sen-
sory input or triggered by neighboring neurons. Then they fire an electri-
cal pulse, which gets picked up by a neighboring dendrite. The dendrite
shoots the electrical charge down the axon. When the charge reaches the
end of the axon, a chemical signal called a neurotransmitter is squirted
out into a small space between the neurons called the synapse (Figure 8).
    Your neurons don’t actually touch each other. Once a neurotransmitter
is released by an axon, it floats around in the synapse until it binds with a
receptor on a neighboring neuron. Then the message continues along in
the same electrical-chemical-electrical pattern. Once its message is
passed along, the neurotransmitter disengages and is either reabsorbed
by the neuron that sent it or broken down to be trashed.




   Figure 8: The dendrite, cell body, axon, myelin sheath, and synapse

   Even though this process might seem a bit complicated, everything
that you think and do is the result of millions of neurons sending electrical
signals, which turn into chemical signals in order to communicate with
each other. The neurons connect in response to experiences we receive
from our senses and the environment.
   As information comes into the brain from your senses, neurons fire and

                        Neuropsychology and Peak Poker Performance

Neuroplasticity: The Mechanism of Brain Change
As we’ve already covered, the critical unit of communication is the neu-
ron, which relies on an electrochemical process to transmit information
through your brain and between your brain and body. All human beings
essentially have the same circuits in their brain, but we differ in the spe-
cific connections between our neurons. We each have unique patterns of
neural activity, and the brain is constantly changing in response to it. Your
brain is not hardwired to make you think or behave in a predetermined
fashion. Instead, your brain changes as you learn new skills or habits using
a process known as neuroplasticity. The end result of learning is that you
multiply your neural connections, which then changes the architecture of
your brain.
    All brains are “plastic” in that they are moldable and change as a result
of experience. You have the power to rewire your brain, at any time –
which is very good news if you want to make new habits or learn new
skills. As I mentioned in Positive Poker, neurons that fire together, wire
together: the more you play poker, the more neurons fire together and
wire together as you improve your skills. The more you play, the more
likely it is that this same circuit of neurons will fire together in the future:
the more you do something, the more likely it is that when you do it again
it won’t take as much effort as it did the previous time. For example, most
players have trouble keeping track of how much money is in the pot when
they first start playing poker. But with practice it becomes easier until
eventually it’s effortless to remember this. This is an example of the neu-
rons wiring together to produce a pot-counting circuit.

Peak Poker Performance

    In fact, every time you learn something new about poker (or anything),
the brain processes that information and establishes fresh neural connec-
tions as networks of neurons fire together. Information comes through
your senses and is processed in the appropriate area. Then, it moves into
the emotional brain via the thalamus, which focuses, screens, and sorts
the information. It sends the information it deems important to the hip-
pocampus, which is responsible for encoding it into memory. The amyg-
dala weighs in on emotionally charged information, which is encoded
more strongly than emotion-neutral material. As we learn and remember,
the same neurons keep firing along the same path, which leads them to
being wired together.
    Finally, if we keep firing neurons enough, our circuits will develop mye-
lination. This is the basis of the 10,000-hour rule of talent development
that I discussed in Positive Poker. Every time you fire a circuit, a tiny
amount of myelin wraps around the neurons. The amount is so small that
it doesn’t make a meaningful difference. But if you keep practicing and
learning, the circuit will keep firing and myelinating. Eventually (10,000
hours later on average), your complete circuit will be fully myelinated and
lightening fast. This is neuroplasticity in a nutshell. Through practice and
learning, your brain changes structure, and you can shape and mold it so
you can succeed at poker.
    Recent studies of people in different occupations (like musicians, chess
players, and athletes) show that the more complex the skills demanded of
the occupation, the greater the number of dendrites found on the neu-
rons. This results in a greater number of connections between neurons
such that messages flow more quickly and efficiently. While poker players
haven’t been studied, specifically, I think it is safe to assume that becom-
ing an expert player encourages dendrite growth.
    Another aspect of neuroplasticity, which is getting quite a bit of press
lately, is something called neurogenesis. For a long time it was believed
that humans were born with all the neurons they would ever have. You
probably remember your high school biology teacher telling you that

them back. While that’s partially true, we now know that there are two

    Both neuroplasticity and neurogenesis are aided by an amazing sub-
stance known as brain-derived neurotrophic factor, a protein which some
scientists describe as being Miracle-Gro for your brain! Others refer to it
as similar to steroids for your brain. It is a powerful substance. If you have
a lot of brain-derived neurotrophic factor in your brain, you’ll learn more
efficiently and have more long-term potential, the process of neurons
firing and wiring together. The really interesting thing about this process
is that long-term potential and brain-derived neurotrophic factor pro-
mote each other, so the more long-term potential you have, the more
brain-derived neurotrophic factor will be produced. Also, when research-
ers deprive the brain of brain-derived neurotrophic factor, learning stops
because long-term potential can no longer happen. This may not sound
too revolutionary on the surface, but trust me it is. It’s a possible brain-
fountain of youth. The rewiring of the brain (neuroplasticity) and the birth
of new neurons (neurogenesis) can be fostered by some essential habits,
which we can all develop. I’ll share more information on this in the next
chapter, but rest assured you have the power to improve your ability to
learn to play better poker, no matter your age.
    Now I would like to take a bit of time to share some information on
neurotransmitters, which I mentioned briefly a couple of times in this
chapter already. They play an important role in your brain health and

Peak Poker Performance

   ♠ dopamine: increases enjoyment, and is necessary to change habits;
       related to motivation
   ♠ serotonin: improves motivation, willpower, and mood; helps you
       sleep well and mediates anxiety
   ♠ norepinephrine: assists with thinking, focus, and dealing with
       stress
   ♠ oxytocin: promotes feelings of love, trust, and connection, and
       reduces anxiety
   ♠ acetylcholine: supports attentiveness and memory
   ♠ glutamate: aids learning and memory
   ♠ gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA): increases feelings of relaxation
       and reduces anxiety
   ♠ melatonin: enhances the quality of sleep
   ♠ endorphins: provides pain relief and feelings of pleasure

   Your brain has systems for all these neurotransmitters. For example,
your dopamine system includes all the neurons that release or react to
dopamine. Your brain relies on numerous neurotransmitter systems for
information processing. While all of the neurotransmitters are important
to optimal functioning, glutamate and GABA carry out as much as 80% of
the communication that occurs in your brain (Ratey, 2008). If any of your
neurotransmitters get out of balance it can lead to states like anxiety, de-
pression, or even lack of motivation.
   Different regions of the brain rely on different neurotransmitters. For
example, the prefrontal cortex relies on serotonin to produce willpower. If
you are low on serotonin, you are likely to be unable to form and adhere
to goals and plans. Low levels of serotonin are also associated with having
more anger and aggression. If you have difficulty concentrating or think-
ing clearly, you are probably low in norepinephrine. Not having enough
dopamine can lead to bad habits and an overall lack of enjoyment.

                         Neuropsychology and Peak Poker Performance

   On the flip side of the coin, boosting serotonin can lead to a better
mood and a greater ability to set and follow through on goals. If your se-
rotonin is balanced, you’ll be more likely to stick to your good habits. An
increase in norepinephrine tends to lead to improved concentration and
overall lower stress levels. More dopamine typically leads to more enjoy-
ment.
   It’s all about balance with the neurotransmitters; it’s not a “more is
better” proposition. Too much dopamine is associated with schizophrenia,
for example, and too little is associated with Parkinson’s disease. It’s super
important to keep your neurotransmitters in balance, and there are many
aspects of diet and exercise that can help. I’ll be covering those in the
next chapter. For now, let’s take a look at how this information can be
used to better understand what is going on in the brain when you experi-
ence tilt.

Your Brain on Tilt
Much has been written in poker literature about where tilt comes from
and what can be done about it. From a pure neuroscience perspective, tilt
(which for our purposes is any strong emotion) is generated by your
amygdala. It works like this: your amygdala registers incoming information
and quickly determines if it is “safe” or “threatening.”
    Once a threat is perceived by your amygdala (which Harvard professor
and psychiatrist John Ratey calls the brain’s panic button), it sets off an in-
voluntary chain reaction in other parts of the brain and body. This puts us
into an alarmed mode and any perceived threat can throw us into a fight or
flight response. Any intense emotional state can trigger a response,
whether it’s anger, sadness, or euphoria. For example, losing a big pot
where you were a “lock” to win but your opponent went runner to beat you
may incite frustration or anger. Even running deep in a multi-table tourna-
ment (MTT) can trigger the amygdala. While running deep is a very good
thing, it can be nail biting, especially if it’s a new experience or if the money
up top is life changing. All this physiological arousal can cause your heart to
race, your perceptual field to narrow, and your palms to get sweaty. It can

Peak Poker Performance

be hard to think clearly and rationally, because so much of your brain’s
processing power is being diverted to attending to the “threat.”
     It’s important to keep in mind that there are two sources of emotions:
external ones, like the gunshot-like sound I heard at the WSOP, and inter-
nal ones. External cues can come from virtually anything in the physical
environment. A sight, a sound, or a physical sensation could all provide the
external cue you need to generate an emotion. Internal causes come from
thoughts or memories. You might remember a terrible beat you took, and
suddenly your mood and physiological state can drastically change. Or if
you are running deep in a major tournament, you could start thinking
about what the money would mean to you, or you might be concerned
about the commentators talking about your play. Either way, these inter-
nal thoughts can trigger a physiological response that dampens focus and
triggers various feeling states.
     To be clear, if your amygdala deems something threatening, it can take
over all bodily functions, before you ever have a chance to “think” about
it. If something is deemed moderately threatening, the amygdala will
communicate to your prefrontal cortex. Your prefrontal cortex will reason
through the information it receives, and if it perceives a need to moder-
ate the emotions that the amygdala generates, it will essentially tell it to
calm down. However, there are a few kinks in the system.
     I’m sure you have noticed that there are times when your rational pre-
frontal cortex loses to the emotional amygdala, and you might be won-
dering why that happens. It’s because there are more connections running
from the amygdala to the prefrontal cortex than there are running from
the prefrontal cortex to the amygdala, so the amygdala is able to send
many more signals to the prefrontal cortex than the prefrontal cortex can
send to it. This point is so important that I want to phrase it another way.
Joseph LeDoux, a world renowned expert on fear, has shown unequivo-
cally that more neural traffic travels from the emotional brain up to the
thinking brain than from the thinking brain down to the emotional brain.
Thus, your emotional brain influences your behavior to a much greater
degree than your thinking brain!

                        Neuropsychology and Peak Poker Performance

    The prefrontal cortex becomes less efficient as it’s further taxed. I
wrote about this at length in Positive Poker. Your prefrontal cortex
houses willpower, which is like a muscle that gets tired with overuse. Also,
it doesn’t work as well if we are tired or hungry, so you can expect to tilt
more anytime you run low on willpower.
    Now that we’ve looked at what happens to your brain when you go on
tilt, let’s turn our attention to another significant problem for poker play-
ers: downswings.

The Neuroscience of Downswings
Bryan Devonshire wrote an article in 2013 titled “It Can Always Get
Worse,” where he discussed how inevitable and common downswings are
if you play No-Limit Hold’Em. Because it’s possible to lose multiple buy-ins
in a very short amount of time, No-Limit Hold’Em can be extremely
swingy in the short term. Of course, over the long haul it’s possible to
beat variance provided you are a good player, but let’s talk about the
emotional side of a downswing and how your brain processes it.
    As human beings, we love to feel we are in control of our own destiny.
Any time we believe we are not in control of our fate, stress usually fol-
lows. Generally speaking, stress is the anxious or threatening feeling that
comes when we interpret a situation as being more than our psychologi-
cal resources can handle. Feeling out of control is one of the most stress-
ful things you can experience, and a downswing certainly fits into this
framework.
    Most players on a downswing describe it as a very negative, depress-
ing, stressful experience. The longer the downswing lasts, the more trou-
bling it becomes. Devonshire (2013) said this about his two-year-long
downswing:

      If I didn’t have other things going on in life, I would be on sui-
      cide watch. If poker was all I did, it would be really easy to fall
      into a deep, dark, depression, figuring everything to be point-
      less during one of these brutal downswings.
